title: Aid cuts drive 28% surge in Rohingya trafficking in Cox's Bazar, UNHCR study finds
excerpt: Sharp reductions in humanitarian funding and essential protection services leave Rohingya refugees and children increasingly vulnerable to human traffickers, joint research warns.

image.alt: Rows of bamboo and tarpaulin shelters in Kutupalong refugee camp, Cox's Bazar
image.credit: John Owens (VOA) / Wikimedia Commons, public domain

content:
Sharp reductions in international humanitarian funding for Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh are directly weakening camp protection systems, leading to a surge in human trafficking, child exploitation and dangerous onward journeys, according to a joint study by the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and researchers at Nuffield College, Oxford University, published on 16 November.

The report, titled Protection on the Edge: How Humanitarian Funding Cuts Increase Trafficking Risks for Rohingya Refugees, documents how simultaneous cutbacks in basic food assistance, shelter maintenance and specialised protection services have dismantled vital defense lines across the 33 congested camps in Cox's Bazar.

Key findings from the study

  • Trafficking surge: Detected human trafficking cases in the Cox's Bazar settlements increased by 28% between 2024 and 2025 as families exhausted negative coping mechanisms.
  • Children heavily impacted: Children accounted for 17% of all detected trafficking victims in 2025, up from 14% in 2024. Between January and September 2026 alone, 411 trafficking victims were formally identified in the camps, with children making up nearly 23% of cases.
  • Population growth vs budget contraction: Between 2024 and 2025, the registered Rohingya refugee population expanded by 17% (adding over 170,000 new arrivals escaping renewed fighting in Myanmar's Rakhine State). In contrast, UNHCR's operational response budget dropped by over 8% in 2025, with further constrained allocations into late 2026.
  • Cuts to protection networks: Legal aid desks, confidential reporting channels, child-friendly spaces and gender-based violence (GBV) response centres have faced staffing and operational cutbacks, leaving traffickers to operate with diminished community oversight.

The compounding crisis

The report highlights that trafficking does not happen in isolation. With the World Food Programme forced to cap monthly food vouchers at $7 to $10 per person and acute malnutrition reaching 14.6%, refugee families are increasingly pressured to send children into informal, hazardous domestic and agricultural labour in neighboring districts, or hand savings over to smugglers organizing perilous boat departures across the Bay of Bengal.

"Humanitarian assistance is not just charity; it is a critical security and protection mechanism," the authors stated. "When basic sustenance and frontline monitoring are slashed, human traffickers immediately fill the void."

Why it matters

The 2026 Joint Response Plan (JRP) for the Rohingya crisis has faced severe shortfalls. While donors often treat protection programmes as secondary to emergency food and shelter, the Oxford-UNHCR study proves that cutting protection desks and child safeguards directly increases exploitation, crime and regional instability.

Sources

  • Protection on the Edge: How Humanitarian Funding Cuts Increase Trafficking Risks for Rohingya Refugees, UNHCR & Nuffield College, University of Oxford, 16 November 2026
